short_title: Municipality of Makati v. Municipality of Taguig
full_title: MUNICIPALITY OF MAKATI (NOW CITY OF MAKATI), PETITIONER, VS. MUNICIPALITY OF TAGUIG (NOW CITY OF TAGUIG), RESPONDENT.

doctrine:
Creating LGUs and fixing their boundaries is a legislative function, so in a boundary dispute the court only **carries legislative intent into effect**. The charters come first. Where the charters do not state the territory in metes and bounds and only adopt historical boundaries (as with Makati and Taguig), the court weighs **historical evidence, maps, cadastral surveys, and the contemporaneous acts of lawful authorities**. It may take judicial notice of official acts of the three branches (Rule 129, Sec. 1). The plaintiff LGU must prove by **preponderance of evidence** that its claim aligns more with legislative intent. The plebiscite requirement first appeared in the 1973 Constitution and applies only prospectively (Ceniza). So the pre-1973 laws and proclamations of the bodies that then controlled boundaries carry great weight. Census results, COMELEC certifications of voting since 1975, and similar documents do not fix boundaries.

Applying by analogy the public international law concept of the **critical date** (when the dispute crystallized), the Court gave little to no probative value to acts done after that date to improve a party's position, unless they were a normal continuation of earlier acts. Here the critical date was January 31, 1990 (Proclamation No. 518), so Makati's 1994 cadastral survey had scarce probative value. **Fort Bonifacio (Parcels 3 and 4, Psu-2031), including the EMBO and Inner Fort barangays, belongs to Taguig.**

On procedure: **the fallo controls over the body of a decision.** The Court's 2016 decision found that Makati had committed forum shopping, but its fallo imposed only contempt fines on Makati's counsel. That decision is presumed to have passed upon dismissal *sub silentio* (Rule 131, Sec. 3(o)), so the CA could not add dismissal of Makati's appeal as a sanction. The Court also reiterated **constitutional avoidance**: it will not rule on constitutionality when the case can be decided on other grounds and the question is not the *lis mota*.
facts:
On November 22, 1993, Taguig sued Makati and national officials in the RTC of Pasig for judicial confirmation of its territory. It claimed that the Enlisted Men's Barangays (EMBOs) and the Inner Fort of Fort Bonifacio (formerly Fort McKinley) were within its territory. It also attacked Proclamation Nos. 2475 (s. 1986) and 518 (s. 1990) as altering its boundaries without the plebiscite required by Art. XI, Sec. 3 of the 1973 Constitution and Art. X, Sec. 10 of the 1987 Constitution. Taguig relied mainly on Survey Plan Psu-2031 (1909), which placed Parcels 3 and 4 of Fort McKinley in Taguig, and on cadastral maps and presidential proclamations. Makati relied on several items: a sketch map its expert drew from an 1891 Spanish registry, the Spanish contract of sale of Hacienda Maricaban, and a 1902 US military map; censuses from 1918 onward; COMELEC certifications that the Inner Fort barangays had voted in Makati since 1975; and its 1994 numerical cadastral survey.

On July 8, 2011, the RTC ruled for Taguig. It confirmed Parcels 3 and 4, Psu-2031 as Taguig's territory, declared the two proclamations unconstitutional, and made permanent the writ of preliminary injunction of August 2, 1994. On July 28, 2011, Makati filed both a motion for reconsideration *ad cautelam* in the RTC and a petition for annulment of judgment in the CA. The pairing judge denied the motion, and Makati appealed (CA-G.R. CV No. 98377). On July 30, 2013, the CA reversed and declared the disputed areas part of Makati. Taguig's motion for reconsideration of that decision was never resolved.

Meanwhile, in *City of Taguig v. City of Makati* (G.R. No. 208393, June 15, 2016), the Supreme Court declared that Makati had engaged in forum shopping by pursuing the annulment petition at the same time as the motion for reconsideration and the later appeal. It held Makati, through its three counsel, guilty of direct contempt and fined each counsel P2,000.00. It did not order the appeal dismissed. Citing that decision, Taguig moved to dismiss Makati's appeal. On March 8, 2017, the CA dismissed the appeal with prejudice for willful and deliberate forum shopping, and it denied reconsideration on October 3, 2017. Makati filed a Rule 45 petition. It invoked transcendental importance and asked that the CA's July 30, 2013 Decision be revived. Taguig answered that the petition raised questions of fact.
issues: Whether the CA erred in dismissing Makati's appeal on the ground of forum shopping.
Whether the Court should resolve the territorial dispute on the merits, including its factual issues, in a Rule 45 petition.
Whether Taguig proved by preponderance of evidence that the disputed areas in Fort Bonifacio are within its territory.
Whether Proclamation Nos. 2475 and 518 should be declared unconstitutional for altering Taguig's boundaries without a plebiscite.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the CA erred.** When the Court found Makati guilty of forum shopping in G.R. No. 208393, it had considered all the arguments, yet it refrained from dismissing the appeal. It "passed upon the dismissal of Makati's appeal *sub silentio*." Under Rule 131, Sec. 3(o), it is presumed that all matters within an issue raised were laid before the court and passed upon by it. If Taguig thought the sanctions insufficient, it should have moved for reconsideration before the ruling became immutable. **The fallo limited Makati's sanction to a fine.** The body of a decision "may be resorted to only to determine the ratio decidendi for the disposition. It should not be taken out of context in order to add to or amend the clear words of the fallo." Where the dispositive portion and the body conflict, the dispositive portion prevails (*BBB v. People*). By dismissing the appeal, the CA "overstepped its bounds."

**2. Yes, the case was resolved on the merits.** Judicial economy required it. The case had dragged on for almost two decades, the records were complete, and a technical dismissal would only invite relitigation. The RTC's and CA's factual findings were "diametrically opposed," which is a recognized exception to the rule that only questions of law are raised under Rule 45 (*Medina v. Asistio, Jr.*). Boundary disputes affect the people's welfare, because an LGU can act only within its territory and its acts beyond it are *ultra vires* (*Mariano v. COMELEC*). They therefore justify relaxing the rules, as in *Municipality of Pateros v. CA*. The charters of both cities also leave existing boundary disputes to "the appropriate agency or forum," which here is the courts.

**3. Yes, Taguig proved its claim.** The power to create LGUs includes the power to fix their boundaries. Under the Philippine Bill of 1902, that power was unlimited. Section 68 of the Revised Administrative Code of 1917 delegated it to the Chief Executive. A plebiscite was first required by the 1973 Constitution, and that requirement is prospective (*Ceniza v. COMELEC*). Courts do not fix territories themselves, since that would be judicial legislation; they only implement the law creating the LGU (*Municipality of Jimenez v. Baz*; *Nueva Era v. Marcos*). Neither city's charter states metes and bounds, however. The Municipal Code of 1901 recognized the pueblos with their existing boundaries, and later laws merely adopted them, so other evidence had to be weighed. Taguig, as plaintiff, had to prove by preponderance of evidence that "its claim aligns more with the intent of the legislature." The Court fixed the **critical date at January 31, 1990**, when Proclamation No. 518 was issued.

(a) *Historical evidence, maps, surveys.* **Psu-2031 was admissible.** Admissibility (relevance and competence) is different from weight. The exhibit was identified by DENR and LRA witnesses and compared with certified true copies, and Makati's counsel stipulated that it was a faithful reproduction. Thirteen proclamations issued from 1957 to 1973 referred to Psu-2031 or used it as their basis. Makati's sketch map, by contrast, was prepared at a party's instance from documents of private proprietary interest. Psu-2031 "carries more weight, impressed as it is with the approval of or adoption by the sovereign itself." The proclamations also treated Parcels 2 and 3 (the 1908 acquisition) as part of Fort McKinley, which defeats Makati's theory that only the 1902 portion was the fort. Makati's own 1979 cadastral map placed Parcel 4 outside Makati, and Taguig's 1983 map included it. Makati's numerical cadastral survey was approved on February 14, 1994, after the critical date and after the suit was filed. It was "of scarce probative value."

(b) *Contemporaneous acts of lawful authorities*, which may be judicially noticed. Section 503 of the 1917 Revised Administrative Code described other camps as "in" or "in or near" named towns but placed Fort McKinley "near Macati." That wording shows the fort was considered entirely outside Makati. Proclamation No. 423 (1957) located the reservation in Pasig, Taguig, Parañaque and Pasay, with Parcel 4 bounded on the north by the Guadalupe Estate. Later proclamations from 1964 to 1987 were similar. Makati appeared as a situs only from 1972 (Proclamation No. 1041), and even then not consistently. Census results "do not, by any stretch of imagination, determine or fix territorial boundaries." The COMELEC certifications prove only political participation since 1975. By then, any change of boundaries required a plebiscite, and none was held except for the cityhood conversions, whose charters deferred to the courts. **Taguig's evidence preponderates, so it has the superior claim to the disputed areas.**

**4. The Court declined to rule on constitutionality.** The proclamations did not expressly alter Taguig's boundaries. They only opened portions of the military reservation to disposition, and their only error was declaring the areas within Makati. Under the policy of **constitutional avoidance** (*Francisco v. House of Representatives*) and the requirement that constitutionality be the *lis mota* (*Parcon-Song v. Parcon*), the case could be decided without that question. The OSG had also not appeared for the Republic, and "[t]he State, as a litigant, is also entitled to due process." **Henceforth the proclamations must be read consistently with this decision: the disputed areas are within Taguig, not Makati.**
disposition:
Petition DENIED. The RTC Decision dated July 8, 2011 was REINSTATED with MODIFICATION:

- Fort Bonifacio Military Reservation, consisting of Parcels 3 and 4, Psu-2031, is confirmed part of the territory of the City of Taguig.
- The Writ of Preliminary Injunction dated August 2, 1994 is made PERMANENT insofar as it enjoins the City of Makati from exercising jurisdiction over, making improvements on, or otherwise treating as part of its territory Parcels 3 and 4, Psu-2031.
- The City of Makati shall pay the costs of suit.

The RTC's declaration that Proclamation Nos. 2475 and 518 are unconstitutional was not carried into the modified judgment.

bar_questions.q: The Cities of Alon and Bato dispute ownership of a former military reservation. Neither city's charter describes its territory by metes and bounds. Each merely adopts its "present territory" and states that it is without prejudice to the resolution by the appropriate forum of existing boundary disputes. Alon sued in 1993. As plaintiff, it presents a 1910 government survey plan of the reservation that places the area in Alon. The plan was approved by the Director of Lands and is cited as basis in a dozen presidential proclamations issued from 1957 to 1972. Bato presents a numerical cadastral survey, approved in 1995, that shows the area within Bato. The dispute had crystallized in 1991, when a presidential proclamation declared the area part of Bato. How should the court weigh these two surveys, and who should prevail?

alac.answer: Alon should prevail. Its 1910 survey plan deserves greater weight, while Bato's 1995 survey has scarce probative value because it was made after the critical date.
alac.legal_basis: In boundary disputes, courts carry into effect the legislative intent expressed in the charters. Where the charters do not define the territory by metes and bounds, the court resorts to historical evidence, maps, cadastral surveys, and contemporaneous acts of lawful authorities. The plaintiff LGU must prove its claim by preponderance of evidence. Applying by analogy the "critical date" concept of public international law, acts done after the dispute crystallized have little to no probative value, unless they are a normal continuation of prior acts and not undertaken merely to improve a party's legal position. A survey plan recognized in official issuances outweighs material prepared at a party's instance. (Municipality of Makati v. Municipality of Taguig, G.R. No. 235316, December 1, 2021)
alac.application: Neither charter fixes the boundary, so the court must weigh the evidence. Alon's 1910 plan was approved by the Director of Lands and repeatedly adopted in presidential proclamations before 1973, when the Chief Executive's acts carried great weight on boundaries. It therefore bears the sovereign's approval. Bato's survey was approved in 1995, after the 1991 critical date and even after Alon sued. Nothing shows it was a normal continuation of earlier acts. It appears to have been prepared to bolster Bato's position, so it deserves scant weight.
alac.conclusion: The court should give greater weight to Alon's survey plan and rule that the area belongs to Alon.

bar_questions.q: In the same case, Bato offers three kinds of evidence: (1) censuses from 1918 to 2010 listing the barangays in the area under Bato; (2) COMELEC certifications that residents of the area have voted in Bato since 1976; and (3) certificates of live birth stating that a hospital inside the area is located in Bato. Alon cites the Revised Administrative Code of 1917, which describes the reservation as located "near Bato" while describing other military camps as "in or near" named towns. It also cites pre-1973 presidential proclamations that locate the reservation in Alon and other towns but never in Bato. No plebiscite has ever been held on the area. Which evidence should prevail? Explain.

alac.answer: Alon's evidence, consisting of laws and presidential proclamations, should prevail over Bato's census results and certifications.
alac.legal_basis: Before the 1973 Constitution, the legislature, and the Chief Executive by delegation under the Revised Administrative Code of 1917, could fix LGU boundaries without a plebiscite. Their contemporaneous acts therefore carry great weight, and courts may take judicial notice of them (Rule 129, Sec. 1). Since the 1973 Constitution, any substantial alteration of boundaries requires approval in a plebiscite (now Art. X, Sec. 10 of the 1987 Constitution). Census results only reflect population statistics and do not fix boundaries. Voting certifications prove only political participation. Laws and proclamations preponderate over census results, COMELEC certifications, and certificates of live birth. (Municipality of Makati v. Municipality of Taguig, G.R. No. 235316, December 1, 2021)
alac.application: The 1917 law used "near Bato" for this reservation, while it used "in or near" for other camps. That shows the lawmaker considered the reservation outside Bato. The pre-1973 proclamations consistently omit Bato as a location. Bato's censuses cannot override these acts of the branches that then controlled boundaries. Its voting certifications begin in 1976, after the plebiscite requirement took effect, and no plebiscite ever transferred the area to Bato. Birth certificates naming Bato as the hospital's location are likewise not acts of the authorities that fix boundaries.
alac.conclusion: The laws and proclamations offered by Alon preponderate, so the area belongs to Alon.

bar_questions.q: In an earlier petition arising from the same boundary case, the Supreme Court discussed in the body of its decision that the City of Bato had committed willful and deliberate forum shopping. Bato had simultaneously pursued a motion for reconsideration in the RTC and a petition for annulment of judgment in the Court of Appeals. The fallo merely declared that Bato engaged in forum shopping, held Bato's lawyers guilty of direct contempt, and fined each of them. No one moved for reconsideration, and the decision became final. Alon then moved in the Court of Appeals to dismiss Bato's pending appeal from the RTC decision, arguing that dismissal is the necessary consequence of willful and deliberate forum shopping. May the Court of Appeals grant the motion?

alac.answer: No. The Court of Appeals cannot dismiss Bato's appeal on a sanction that the Supreme Court's fallo did not impose.
alac.legal_basis: The dispositive portion, or fallo, is the operative part of a decision. Where it conflicts with the body, the fallo controls, and the body may be consulted only to find the ratio decidendi, not to add to or amend the fallo. Under Rule 131, Sec. 3(o), it is presumed that all matters within an issue raised were laid before the court and passed upon by it. A sanction the Court considered but did not impose is deemed passed upon sub silentio. A party dissatisfied with the sanctions must seek reconsideration before the ruling becomes immutable. (Municipality of Makati v. Municipality of Taguig, G.R. No. 235316, December 1, 2021)
alac.application: When the Supreme Court found forum shopping, it had the whole controversy before it and chose to sanction only Bato's lawyers with contempt fines. The dismissal of Bato's appeal is presumed to have been considered and rejected. The finding of forum shopping in the body cannot be used to add a dismissal that the fallo does not contain. Alon did not seek reconsideration, so the decision, with its limited sanction, became final. By dismissing the appeal, the Court of Appeals would be overstepping that final judgment.
alac.conclusion: The Court of Appeals should deny Alon's motion and resolve Bato's appeal on the merits.

notes: Two maps reproduced in the decision are missing from the E-Library text (marked "image supposed to be here"); the reasoning is fully legible without them. The long trial transcripts quoted in the decision are omitted here. The index has no separate resolution on a motion for reconsideration of this decision. The decision dates Proclamation No. 1041 inconsistently: June 29, 1970 in the list of pre-1973 issuances citing Psu-2031, and June 29, 1972 in the discussion of contemporaneous acts. Among Makati's evidence, the decision also lists a certification that the Inner Fort barangays receive real property tax shares from Makati, but the ruling does not weigh it separately.
